Idi Amin. Uganda's military dictator from 1971 to 1979, notorious for his brutality, arbitrary violence, and economic destruction. A brutal autocrat whose regime killed an estimated 300,000 people through executions, torture, and persecution, he became a symbol of African despotism and was eventually overthrown by Tanzanian-backed forces.

He rose from military ranks to seize power in a 1971 coup, overthrowing President Milton Obote and promising reform but quickly descending into random terror and ethnic persecution. He created secret police and execution squads that tortured and murdered political opponents, intellectuals, clergy, and ethnic minorities, particularly the Acholi and Lango peoples. In 1972, he expelled Uganda's entire Asian population—Indians and Pakistanis—confiscating their property and destabilizing the economy through discriminatory nationalist ideology and personal greed. He declared himself President for Life and adopted increasingly grandiose titles, ruling through fear, ethnic favoritism concentrating power among his Kakwa ethnic group, and economic collapse.

In 1979, he invaded and occupied the Tanzanian Kagera salient, triggering military intervention by Julius Nyerere's Tanzania. This ousted him after eight years of terror. He fled into exile in Libya and Saudi Arabia, dying in hiding in Jidda, Saudi Arabia, in 2003. He is remembered as one of Africa's most brutal postcolonial dictators, contrasting sharply with Nyerere, the Tanzanian leader whose forces ended his dictatorship, and echoing the authoritarianism of Robert Mugabe and Kwame Nkrumah, earlier African leaders whose authoritarian patterns foreshadowed his own.
